argument:
Plotinus lived in the Roman world of about 250 AD, in what historians call the crisis of the third century. War and plague were constant. Stephen West notes that the population of the region is thought to have fallen by a third, and that the survivors still had to pay for the wars. Taxes soared, and people who could not pay were forced to leave and walk somewhere else. Philosophy made its largest strides here, as it had a couple of hundred years earlier in the Hellenistic age, under political collapse.

Something quieter had shifted too. Earlier Greek thinkers mostly treated the soul as compatible with the physical world, as much a part of you as your hands, the part that reasons or feels. By Plotinus' time, more and more people saw themselves instead as a consciousness imprisoned in a flawed body inside a flawed realm, waiting to get back to a higher one. Your body belongs to you the way a smartphone does, but it is not you. The host likens the mood to crash-landing on a hostile alien planet and scrounging parts to fly home. Christianity was rising in that same soil, offering personal salvation. Borrowing from Luc Ferry's A Brief History of Thought, the host separates religion from philosophy: humans alone dread irreversibility, and religion answers by calling death an illusion, while philosophy is salvation without religion, built from human means alone.

So imagine carrying the obvious objection to Plotinus, the respected sage of the age: how can a good and powerful God allow evil? He would say evil does not exist, not the way you mean. Bad things are absences of good. Voldemort commits his evil acts only because he has a working body and enough health to chase Harry around, and even his ruined nose is good enough to breathe through. Strip away every good quality and the thing could not exist at all. Plotinus was consistent about the physical world's second-rate status. Asked to sit for a portrait, he replied, "Is it not enough to have to carry around this image? Must I transmit the image of this image as worthy of attention?"

The rest follows from unity. Nothing is a thing without it: no army, no chorus, no house, no ship. A dog's unity is inherent, a clock's was assembled by a clockmaker, a marching band has less still. The more unity, the more real. Plotinus stacks this into a chain of being, pictured as a three-tiered fountain. The One, beyond description, overflows into the Intellect, which holds the perfect forms, pure tree-y-ness with no greenness attached. The Intellect overflows into the Soul, which casts reflections of those forms into crude matter. Our world is a Polaroid of a Polaroid of a Polaroid, which is why good arrives here diluted.

The advice, then, is to turn away from bodily existence and contemplate the forms. The host flags unity and the hierarchy as what to carry into later Christian and Catholic philosophy, and closes by asking what adversity shaped you.
keyIdeas: Plotinus's privation theory holds that evil is not a presence but an absence of goodness; nothing can be wholly evil because complete absence of good would mean the thing couldn't exist at all.

Existence itself counts as a good, so anything that exists -- even something monstrous -- retains some minimal good (like basic functioning) that allows it to exist, blocking the idea of 'pure evil' as its own positive force.
Plotinus grounds his whole system in the question of what makes something one thing rather than a mere aggregate: an army, a chorus, or a ship needs real unity to exist as what it's called.

The more unity something possesses, the more real it is -- reality is graded rather than binary, producing a hierarchy of being: natural unity (like a dog's) ranks above artificially assembled unity (like a clock's), and the pure Form of a thing ranks above any physical instance mixing multiple qualities together.

This graded hierarchy reframes evil as a deficiency or falling-away from unity/coherence/goodness, rather than as an independently existing force -- explaining the problem of evil without denying that bad things happen.
